subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1947-48  REINSTATE- MENT AND COMPENSATION
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1947-48  REINSTATE- MENT AND COMPENSATION
speechtext:
This bill adds a new
section to the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act. The object of the new section is indicated therein-to give power to the board to make an order requiring an employer to reinstate any employee discharged contrary to the provisions of the act, and to pay such employee the monetary loss suffered by reason of such discharge.

speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill No. 11, to amend the Dominion Elections Act, 1938 (age of voters).

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REDUCE THE ELIGIBLE AGE OF VOTERS FROM 21 TO 18
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REDUCE THE ELIGIBLE AGE OF VOTERS FROM 21 TO 18
speechtext:
The purpose of this bill is to
take into account the superior education and training now given Canadian youth; also the fact that at eighteen years of age Canadians are considered sufficiently mature to serve in the country's armed forces. It therefore seeks to amend the Dominion Elections Act by reducing the eligible voting age from twenty-one to eighteen.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REDUCE THE ELIGIBLE AGE OF VOTERS FROM 21 TO 18

Seven is the age of wisdom.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO ADDRESS OF GENERAL MCNAUGHTON TO CANADIAN GEOGRAPHICAL SOCIETY

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: REFERENCE TO ADDRESS OF GENERAL MCNAUGHTON TO CANADIAN GEOGRAPHICAL SOCIETY
speechtext:
I should like to answer a question asked by the leader of the opposition on Monday, about a speech delivered by General McNaughton to the Canadian Geographical Society. I had told him that I had not had an opportunity of reading the text of this speech. Since then I have been able to do so and to discuss it with my colleague the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton).
I am now prepared to answer the question.
Hon. members will recall that the question read as follows:
. . . whether the speech made by General A. G. L. McNaughton to the annual meeting of the Canadian Geographical Society in Ottawa on Friday, February 24, was authorized by the Department of National Defence or any other department of the Canadian government. Whether authorized or not, does the government now approve the statements contained in that speech?
There was no official authorization, because the occasion did not call for any official authorization. For some time General McNaughton has been a member of the Canadian Geographical Society. He was speaking to the fellows of that society, and stated in express terms that he was giving them his personal opinion, as appears at page 19 of his text:
I would emphasize that what I have to say represents my personal opinions alone.
Nevertheless I read with a great deal of interest, as I am sure the hon. member did, the text of the speech. After doing so, and discussing it with my colleague the Minister of National Defence, I have to say that we are in full agreement with the views General McNaughton expressed on that occasion.
The leader of the opposition directed my attention particularly to one paragraph which reads as follows:
It is on the peaceful aspects of co-operation, current and long term, that I feel that emphasis should be placed in the organization and functions of the commonwealth-much more so, perhaps, than on the commonwealth as an arrangement for the collective security of its members, which by itself under existing circumstances and present dangers it is not well adapted to undertake. In this connection, with the entry of Newfoundland into confederation we have assumed full responsibility for the solution of the significant problems of the defence of our Atlantic seaboard.
That last sentence, of course, is a statement of fact. That part of our Atlantic seaboard has now become a part of Canada, and it is our primary responsibility to defend our own shores. I believe that paragraph has to be considered with the rest of the text. So

that it may be understood, I believe the part of the text of which that is one paragraph should be placed on the record.
General McNaughton had been discussing the operations of the permanent joint board on defence; the simultaneous declaration about defence made in this house and in Washington, by my predecessor, as prime minister, and the President of the United States in February, 1947; and the establishment in April, 1948, of the joint United States-Canada industrial mobilization committee. He described how they functioned, and then went on:
With these provisions for the free and intimate discussion of defence matters which are of mutual concern to Canada and to the United States, and for their orderly conduct, no one in either of our countries, or in any other country, need fear that any of the precautions essential to the security of North America are being neglected.
As I have said, Canada, like the United States, is fully aware that its security does not rest on the protection of the territory of that continent alone. We realize that this requires continued association with other peoples of good will, who, like ourselves, are devoted to the cause of peace.
In the first place there is the commonwealth. In addition to being a nation of the American continent, and now a member of the Atlantic pact, Canada is also a member of the commonwealth, and she holds to that association with all the firm conviction which has marked the course of our history since early times. She holds to that association as a nation in her own right, exercising full sovereign powers, and happy to co-operate in all matters which make for peace and orderly progress in the commonwealth and in the world.
There are some who may see a difficulty in reconciling our position as a nation on the American continent with our membership in the commonwealth; others may be still further disturbed as to our relation to the commonwealth in consequence of our entry into an Atlantic pact, but I do not share these anxieties.
In the first place, I believe that fundamentally the real interests of the member nations of the commonwealth are very close to those of the United States and likewise to those of the democratic countries of Europe now associated in the Atlantic pact. We all stand firmly for peace, for individual freedom and for democracy as the proper form of government. In the second place, I think we are a practical people ready to deal with each question as it arises on its merits and on the basis of the facts. We see no reason for conflict in interest, and every reason for co-operation between the commonwealth and the United States and with western Europe, and you can be quite sure, with our deep concern for the welfare of each of these great associations of peoples with whom we are so intimately linked, we in Canada will devote ourselves on every occasion to promoting unanimity in view.
Then the paragraph to which reference was made follows:
It is on the peaceful aspects of co-operation, current and long term, that I feel that emphasis should be placed in the organization and functions of the commonwealth-much more so, perhaps, than on the commonwealth as an arrangement for the collective security of its members, which by itself under existing circumstances and present dangers it is not well adapted to undertake. In this connection, with the entry of Newfoundland into coninquiries of the Ministry
federation we have assumed full responsibility for the solution of the significant problems of the defence of our Atlantic seaboard.
I believe that is in line with the policy that has been expressed over the years, not only by the members of this government but by representatives of the other commonwealth nations. We do not regard the commonwealth as a defence alliance. As a matter of fact, unfortunately under present conditions and dangers it is not the fitting organization to provide adequate security for each of its members. That was clearly expressed by my predecessor in an address which he delivered to the members of both houses of parliament of the United Kingdom on May 11, 1944, from which I would merely quote these short paragraphs:
Like the nations of which it is composed, the British commonwealth has within itself a spirit which is not exclusive but the opposite of exclusive. Therein lies its strength. That spirit expresses itself in co-operation. Therein lies the secret of its unity. Co-operation is capable of indefinite expansion. Therein lies the hope of the future.	(
It is of the utmost importance to the commonwealth that there should continue to be the greatest possible co-operation among its members. In like manner it is, I believe, of the utmost importance to the future of mankind that, after the war, there should be the greatest possible co-operation among the nations of the world.
Our wartime co-operation is not the product of formal institutional unity; it is the result of agreement upon policies of benefit to all. Moreover, they are policies that make an appeal "to all sorts of men in all sorts of countries," provided only they are men of good will.
If, at the close of hostilities the strength and unity of the commonwealth are to be maintained, those ends will be achieved not by policies which are exclusive, but by policies which can be shared with other nations. I am firmly convinced that the way to maintain our unity is to base that unity upon principles which can be extended to all nations. I am equally sure that the only way to maintain world unity is to base it upon principles that can be universally applied.
The war has surely convinced all nations, from the smallest to the greatest, that there is no national security to be found in the isolation of any nation or group of nations. The future security of peace-loving nations will depend upon the extent and effectiveness of international co-operation.
That has been repeated time and again by members of this government. As I read General McNaughton's speech, it is an able and well-expressed statement of the same views.

Mr. Speaker, when the house adjourned last night I said that if our farmers were given the necessary encouragement, as in the past, our sons would not be apt to leave the soil. Since I have only a few minutes remaining I feel it is my duty to continue on a very important question, and to express my views on our natural resources. I believe it is the duty of all hon. members to bend their efforts toward the development of our natural resources for the good of our coming generations. Providence has provided Canada with tremendous natural resources for our future generations. Each province has different natural resources, and I believe it would be regrettable if we neglected to develop these resources for the benefit of our people.
It is our duty to spare no expense in order to develop our natural resources so that our younger element will realize that those wh* are in charge of the affairs of this country have provided for their future and have made it possible for them to share in the future prosperity of Canada. I believe that every hon. member in this house will support the government in its efforts to develop our natural resources. In this country we
360	HOUSE OF COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Gosselin have a population of which we should be proud. We should feel confident that they will carry on in the future to the best of their ability. In the past we have shown that we can be united. Unity is the basis upon which the prosperity of the country depends. The example which was given to us by our soldiers during the last war proves that unity and good understanding assure us of that prosperity which we desire and which we appreciate so much.
My time is just about exhausted. I feel that I should call on all hon. members to unite and to carry on in the best way possible to assure our people that whatever is necessary to provide for their future and welfare will be done. I regret that the time allotted to me does not permit me to continue with what I feel would be a remedy for some of our ills. I still believe that the present government is not neglecting in any way to provide that which is necessarv to provide for the future of Canadians.
I wish to say a few words about unemployment. At the present time, Mr. Speaker, unemployment may appear to be disastrous, but as we look around us we realize that the difficulties of the people are not those which they have experienced in the past. Our people face the future with confidence. They are well aware that adjustment is necessary. They are well aware that the government has to proceed with caution. Our government has to proceed in such a way that its acts will be beneficial, and it is providing security measures against the aggressor. Our people are proud of its actions, because they feel that our enormous wealth will be distributed if possible. Let us join together and give our people the assurance that we are working for their welfare, that we are working to provide for every one of our people and that there is a future for them. By so doing I believe we will be establishing a principle whereby we will be guaranteeing the matter of financing. We will be guaranteeing the future prosperity of those in our country who look to us for an assurance of their welfare and of the opportunity to make an honest living. We will also create friendship in the United Kingdom and throughout Europe among those who look to us to perpetuate the principles for which our soldiers fought so valiantly.
I must now conclude my remarks because the time at my disposal is exhausted. I do so however in the expectation that I shall have the opportunity to join in other debates upon those occasions when I may feel that I can express myself for the benefit of those whom J have the honour tc represent.

Mr. Speaker, rising to take part in the debate I should like first to extend my congratulations to the mover (Mr. Larson) and the seconder (Mr. Dumas) of the address in reply. In my opinion this is a well-deserved promotion and, for my part, I wish him every success.
I was sorry to hear the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Gregg) state the other day in answer to a question that it was not his intention to set up a committee on veterans affairs at this session. Most hon. members are aware that the Legion has presented to the government a brief which deals with various matters connected with veterans affairs, a brief which could very well be considered by the committee.
The announcement has been made in the press that the minister will introduce at this session certain amendments to the War Veterans Allowance Act. These amendments could be considered by the committee. Then, there appears on the order paper a resolution standing in the name of the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond (Mr. Goode) which states:
That in the opinion of this house the government should give early consideration as to the advisability of increasing the basic rates of the war veterans allowance to $50 per month for single veterans and widows, and $85 per month for married veterans and widows with dependent children.
Anyone who looks over the large number of resolutions already appearing on the order paper will agree I am sure that there is no hope of this most important resolution being considered by the house at this session. If the minister would reconsider his decision and set up a committee, the subject matter of this resolution could be given every consideration. At the last committee on veterans affairs this subject was considered and certain conclusions arrived at. It is my honest opinion, and I believe that of many veteran members in the house, that those conclusions were slightly in error, and that the committee should be given an opportunity to make the necessary change.
If however the minister has finally decided that he does not intend to recommend the setting up of the committee, I would suggest to him that he advise hon. members who are interested in veterans affairs-and that would include every hon. member, no matter where he sits-just why he has chosen to refuse to have the committee set up.
At the last session of parliament, just before armistice day, I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) if it was to be considered

a legal holiday, and whether or not the house would sit on that day. The Prime Minister replied that armistice day was a legal holiday, but that the house would sit as usual.
The matter of establishing armistice day as a legal holiday has been considered by various sections of the Legion in my district, and the members of the Legion feel that it should be observed in Canada as a national holiday in the same manner as we observe Good Friday, Christmas, Labour day and other holidays. Armistice day has a deep significance to the majority of people in Canada. However, when the government does not choose to observe it as a national holiday one cannot complain very much when the rest of the country fails to do so.
I have received a copy of a resolution passed by the county council of the county of Hastings, in which I reside, asking that armistice day be observed as a national holiday. I trust that before next November arrives the government will have taken some action to see that this day of remembrance is observed as a national holiday.
While we are speaking about holidays I would suggest to the government the advisability of having all holidays, with the exception of Christmas, Good Friday and armistice day, observed on the Monday closest to the day on which the holiday falls. A statutory holiday in the middle of a week is of little benefit to many people. On the other hand a holiday on a week end, preferably on Monday, not only gives a long week end but makes possible the taking of trips by many people who would not be able to do so if the holiday were permitted to remain in the middle of the week. I understand such a change would involve only a slight amendment to the Bills of Exchange Act. I suggest to the government that these matters referring to the holding of holidays on Mondays and the observance of armistice day as a national holiday be seriously considered.
I would bring to the attention of the Minister of Veterans Affairs the rumoured proposal that the office of the Department of Veterans Affairs in Peterborough be closed. This office serves a large number of veterans in that area, and if it is closed it will be necessary for them to do their business and have their consultations with veterans affairs offices either at Toronto or at Kingston. In many cases, the necessity of travelling to either of these centres would involve long, expensive and sometimes most inconvenient trips. Before the office is closed I hope the minister will give serious consideration to the inconvenience which would be caused to the large number of veterans in that area who take advantage of the Peterborough office.

(1)	When cheese is assembled in large quantities it enables the producers to classify it according to indications of good keeping qualities, freedom from foreign material and other physical characteristics, and sell it according to classifications, which should encourage competitive buying as the trade could be provided with their preferred requirements.
(2)	It also provides the producers with a building in which to store their cheese should the market at any time appear unsettled and unfavourable.

In addition to a large amount of cheese, Hastings county also produces many other farm products including a large number of pork products. As Hastings county is largely an agricultural district it is only natural that the farmer producers are most keenly and vitally interested in the falling prices affecting their products. Agriculture is the most basic industry in the world. It produces the greater portion of the food required to feed the world, and Canada despite its industrial growth is primarily an agricultural country. It is one of the few countries left in the world in which

so do not pass through that office. When one considers that Hastings is an agricultural county, the presence of several thousand unemployed there would hardly bear out those glowing advertisements which appeared before the election.
For nearly ten years the government has sold all the farmers' produce. My county is particularly interested in cheese; and that cheese was requisitioned by the government. With the scarcity of food during the war it was not difficult to sell any farm product; but now that our markets have faded away, and when we are faced with the additional difficulty in connection with the convertibility of sterling, it seems that the whole problem of marketing farm products is to be dumped back into the lap of the farmer producer, and this despite the fact that everyone recognizes that the Canadian farmer made a great contribution to our war effort. The farmer producer was told during the war period that he would be assured of future markets, and in many cases he was forced to accept for his product a price which was below the world market price. So I suggest to the minister that some step must be taken to cushion the shock during this readjustment period.
A drop in farm prices will affect a large number of Canadian veterans who have used their gratuities and re-establishment credits to get started on farms. All these veterans have made heavy financial commitments; and if they are to be successfully re-established in our peacetime economy they must receive a fair and just return on their investment and fair prices for the commodities they produce. If we in Canada, Mr. Speaker, wish to keep all Canadians fully employed, and maintain our standard of living, then I submit that the farmer producer must be put on a basis somewhat comparable to labour. He must receive a fair and equitable return, not only on his investment but on his labour as well.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the amendment to the amendment moved by the member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). I wish to deal particularly with the first two clauses of that amendment, as found on page 68 of Hansard, which read as follows:
We respectfully submit to Your Excellency that Your Excellency's advisers have:
(1)	failed to take adequate measures to preserve and expand markets for Canada's surplus products of farm, forest, sea and mine, and to deal with the problems of increasing unemployment and reduced income to Canadian farmers and other producers: and
(2)	failed to take steps to inaugurate an over-all social security program including national health insurance and the removal of the means test from the old age pension:
Before proceeding with my remarks on the amendment to the amendment, I wish to express my support of the remarks of the member for Rosetown-Biggar, my leader, concerning the international situation, when he was speaking on this address. Without a doubt, thoughtful people everywhere are seriously concerned about international developments. While there is widespread concern over the loss of markets, and unemployment, recent information concerning the hydrogen bomb and its terrible possibilities has focused the attention of the average Canadian, as well as average people everywhere, on the urgent necessity for international control of this frightful weapon of war. I agree, Mr. Speaker, with the member for Rosetown-Biggar when he said there were two alternatives facing us. This is reported at page 66 of Hansard of February 20, and reads as follows:
One Is to despair, to organize our side of the Iron curtain and engage In a furious and intolerable armament race; the other is to bend every effort to find an acceptable plan for international control and inspection, and proceed at the same time to remove from the world the age-old causes of war.
The evidence of growing concern about the development of this terrible weapon comes from many quarters, and those quarters are increasing from day to day. As has been said before, Senator McMahon, the

joint chairman of the United States congressional committee on atomic energy, has made a generous and worth-while proposal. According to his calculations, the United States is spending $15 billion a year on armaments and war preparedness. Quite recently, he proposed that the United States might give a lead by offering the world, through the United Nations, two-thirds of that sum for five years on two conditions. His first condition was a general acceptance of a satisfactory program for the effective control of atomic energy. The second condition was agreement by all countries, enforced by inspections, that two-thirds of their present spending on armaments be used for constructive purposes.
This proposal, Mr. Speaker, continues to receive surprising support from all groups in the United States. It has been welcomed by many individuals and groups in Canada as well as in other countries. In my opinion, the generous spirit of this proposal should receive every encouragement from the government of Canada.
As an indication of the thinking of many Canadians, I wish to quote briefly from some newspapers. I do this because the editorial I wish to read now puts in brief and concrete terms what I have found in letters written to me, and what I have discovered in conversation with my constituents. I am here to present the views of my constituents, Mr. Speaker, so I want to quote an editorial that appeared in the Kootenaian, February 16, 1950. It reads as follows:
Peace cannot be secured through bombs
After the first world war the sincere efforts for world peace of the league of nations were sabotaged by the ruthless agents of International capitalists living in London and New York. Such men in the United States broke Wilson's heart when they steered the support of their country even from membership in the league of nations, and, as they were the world's richest nation, this action resulted in the failure of the league to achieve lasting world peace.
The winning of the second world war was followed by the forming of the United Nations Assembly with whom the establishment of world peace has been entrusted. But the failure of Russia to agree with the western democracies on terms seems to have resulted in stalemate again and there is open talk of a third world war. Entrenched behind possession of the A bomb by the United States, we have been lulled to rest by the fact of United States military might.
We do not wish to enter into an argument over who is right and who is wrong. As we pointed out in our last issue, the great majority of humans in all nations want lasting peace, but it seems that the extremists in both camps keep us from arriving on ground where this can be attained. Is it not inevitable that militarists are the worst possible men to be entrusted with our world peace discussions? And does anyone doubt but that the international armament trusts are again using their large financial powers to keep peace from being established?
The Address-Mr. Herridge
Science up to now has given its discoveries to the entire world, irrespective of national boundaries. Prominent scientists of Egypt, Greece, Italy, France, Germany, Britain, United States and Canada have all contributed to the sum of scientific information that is used universally today for man's welfare.
Now come the A bomb and the H bomb, and they are being treasured up as bolsters to ensure peace. It just won't work. Already the Russians seem to have caught up with the United States in bomb manufacture; and when we imagine them in first place in atomic research, we are brought face up to the futility of such securities for peace.
True peace is a world away from the enthroned materialism which finds expression in militarism and lethal weapons. Peace is the natural expression of culture; it is of the spirit-the spirit of Christianity. We are living (or are we?) in Christian countries; so, if there is any sincerity in our search for peace, why do we not entrust the Christian church with a fair share of the work of establishing it? In our opinion the main missionary strength of the church today should be turned against the pagan influences in our governments and diplomacy, which are gradually but surely driving the world into the biblical Armageddon.
I quote that, Mr. Speaker, because it contains, in brief, passages from many of the letters I have received from a number of people.
Before proceeding further, I should like to quote from the Rural Co-operator, Toronto, February 14, as follows:
But we do believe that peace should be sought at almost any price. We believe that peace in our time cannot be had without paying some price, and with the ever-more-terrifying prospects of the consequences of another war we believe that even a very high price for peace is worth considering.
Then, in conclusion, I see in this morning's Ottawa Citizen a news item headed "York calls for talks on H-bomb", which reads in part as follows:
Dr. Cyril Garbett, Archbishop of York and second highest dignitary of the Church of England, yesterday appealed for an immediate attempt "on the highest level" to reach agreement with Russia on the hydrogen bomb.
Those editorials, Mr. Speaker, and those requests by leading churchmen and church groups, reflect a growing opinion all over the world that our countries on the western side of this world must make every effort possible to see if an agreement cannot be reached before we go on with the greater development of these terrifying weapons of war. In my opinion the belief that the world crisis can be resolved merely by resisting and containing communism is a delusive one. Many have persuaded themselves that this resistance and this containment must take precedence over everything and that Canadian social objectives even must not only be subordinated to the work of containment but, if some people had their way, in many fields sacrificed.
To anyone who is greatly concerned with the whole world situation, and the trend of

For the information of the house I wish to quote briefly from an article in The Atlantic of August, 1949, entitled "The conquest of America" by Archibald MacLeish, professor at Harvard.
Everyone who has followed that gentleman knows of his high position in the United States and the great contribution he has made there to education and culture. I would advise everyone to read the article because it contains a great deal of thoughtful material.
I read these excerpts because they indicate clearly the dangers that can develop within a democratic society owing to the fears engendered because of the possibility of aggression of other powers:
The inadequacy of the position we have taken, even within its own narrow and negative purpose, is only too obvious. Neither communism nor any other body of positive belief can be overcome in a period of world-wide dissatisfaction and unrest merely by denying it, or by offering, as a substitute, the world of things as they are. It can be fought only by facing it with a true alternative. And the true alternative to communism is not the world of things as they are; nor, even more certainly, is it some other kind of authoritarianism.
The real choice is the choice between all forms of authoritarianism on the one side and, on the other, the dream of a whole and responsible human freedom. . . .
For, by putting the hatred and fear of Russia first we have opened the sacred centre of our lives, our most essential freedoms-the freedoms of mind and thought-to those among us who have always hated those freedoms and who know well how to use our fear of Russia as a mass to cover their disguise attacks. The spread of legalized thought control from points of infection in the congress to state legislature after state legislature across the country is not the work of chance. It is the work of freedom-hating men. And we have laid the nation open to them by our fears ....
It will not be possible for us to argue, when the finger of time is levelled against us, that we did not see what needed to be done. The wisest and soberest and most realistic statesman of our generation warned us three years ago that the job we had to do-the job we had to do whether there were communists around or not-was to make freedom a reality in the post-war world; and Henry L. Stimson did not speak alone.
As one of my correspondents I think so rightly said, at this time if to these problems we are going to have, shall I say, a collective approach which is wider than the bounds of political parties or wider than the bounds of various religious beliefs and faiths, we need a positive and dynamic Christian approach to meet effectively the problems that face us at home and abroad.
