I wish now, Mr. Speaker, to deal briefly with the first clause of the amendment to the amendment which reads as follows:
(1) failed to take adequate measures to preserve and expand markets for Canada's surplus products of farm, forest, sea and mine, and to deal with the problems of increasing unemployment and reduced income to Canadian farmers and other producers;
Before I conclude I think I can produce evidence which will justify on sound ground the supporting of this amendment to the amendment moved by my leader, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). The loss of markets and the growing unemployment are evidence of the government's failure to give effect to its former pledges and promises. On that basis, this amendment is fully justified.
First of all, going back to 1945, we had the political promises of the government made during the 1945 election. Throughout this country we had large posters which said "Vote for a new social order", which implied a new social order. In the recent election we had1 posters which said "Vote for more jobs for more people" and posters which said "Vote for markets and prosperity". In my opinion this government, since 1946, has completely changed direction in its attitude to the question of full employment and the question of foreign markets. I shall attempt to prove that statement by a few quotations from various official documents. First of all, article 55 of the United Nations charter has this to say:
With a view to the creation of conditions of stability and well-being which are necessary for peaceful and friendly relations among nations based on respect for the principle of equal rights and self-determination of peoples, the United Nations shall promote:
(a)	higher standards of living, full employment and conditions of economic and social progress and development;
(b)	solutions of international economic, social, health, and related problems; and international cultural and educational co-operation; and
(c)	universal respect for, and observance of, human rights and fundamental freedoms for all without distinction as to race, sex, language or religion.
Then article 56 reads as follows:
All members pledge themselves to take joint and separate action in co-operation with the organization for the achievement of the purposes set forth in article 55.
We must not forget that our government signed the charter of the United Nations.
Then we come to the white book on "Employment and Income" tabled in this house by Right Hon. C. D. Howe, Minister of Trade and Commerce, early in 1945. I just want to quote from that document briefly:
It has not been possible during the war to accumulate a large "shelf" of ready-planned public projects. The war program has necessarily taken

precedence and the engineering staffs of all governments have been denuded by war demands. Particularly has it been impossible to embark on the planning of new types of comprehensive projects of far-reaching extent. On the other hand, all governments, dominion, provincial and municipal, have a considerable backlog of public projects of the normal sort for maintenance and expansion, which have been deferred during the war years. Some of these are fully planned and others are capable of rapid planning. Governments will wish to carry out these projects as soon as labour and materials are available once more . . .
Accordingly, as an appropriate policy for this period, the dominion proposes to press ahead with the planning of its own deferred works and invites provinces and municipalities to do the same . . .
The deliberate use of public investment expenditures as a permanent instrument in employment policy has to be undertaken experimentally.
Now, after five years, we learn that this program, as set forth in this white paper, has not been fulfilled. We come into an unemployment situation in which the government admits that it has no shelf of public projects planned over a period of years, as there should have been, to which effect could be given when unemployment arose. I will admit that in previous years in the immediate past there was not the necessity to use this shelf of public works; but in 1945 we were promised by this government that they were making plans for a shelf of public works to use as soon as necessary.
I read the Prime Minister's speech carefully. After reading that speech I would say that there is concrete evidence there of a change in direction in government policy since 1945. In 1945 there was emphasis on the necessity for public investment to maintain full employment. Now without question, this government, believing in free enterprise as it does, is emphasizing the ability of private enterprise to provide employment. We must not forget this. Regardless of what the supporters of private or free enterprise, as it is called, say, free enterprise always comes to government to rescue the casualties of unemployment.
What were the proposals of the government of Canada in the green books of August, 1945, Mr. Speaker? I quote again:
In familiar terms, our objectives are high and stable employment and income and a greater sense of public responsibility for individual economic security and welfare. Realization of these objectives for all Canadians, as Canadians, is a cause in which we would hope for national enthusiasm and unity.
The government has clear and definite views on how these objectives can be attained. These views may be summarized very briefly as,
First, to facilitate private enterprise to produce and provide employment;
Secondly, to promote bold action by the state in those fields in which the public interest calls for public enterprise in national development;
The Address-Mr. Herrtdge
Thirdly, to provide, through public investment, productive employment for our human and physical resources when international and other conditions adversely affect employment; and
Fourthly, to provide, on the basis of small regular payments against large and uncertain individual risks, for such hazards and disabilities as unemployment, sickness and old age.
It is quite safe to say, Mr. Speaker, that the government has not taken bold action with respect to providing a shelf of employment projects, and it certainly has not brought before this parliament so far an overall security scheme.
On the basis of this government's statements, on the basis of public statements in the press, speeches by members of this government in 1945 and in the preceding years, 1943 on, various provincial governments in Canada were stimulated to make plans with respect to the post-war rehabilitation period. I know that in the province of British Columbia, as a result of action by the legislature, we formed the post-war rehabilitation council of British Columbia. There was a great deal of enthusiasm and unity concerning the possibilities of joint action between the federal, provincial and municipal governments for the development of an economic order that would provide full employment and markets for agricultural products. That post-war rehabilitation council travelled all over British Columbia. It received briefs from municipal councils; it went to a great deal of trouble to prepare briefs, to outline schemes of development and possibilities for work over the years. It received the same co-operation from trade unions, co-operative organizations and veterans' organizations. I can say that the whole community in British Columbia co-operated to present their views to this post-war rehabilitation council; and without any doubt those efforts were put forth, and that very comprehensive report was drafted, in the belief that this government was going to take the lead in a public investment program in co-operation with provincial and municipal governments. I may say I was a member of the provincial legislature at that time. When we were discussing this question the question of public works was brought to the attention of the government, and it was said that $210 million was to be used for the development of roads and highways. The question came up in the legislature as to how it was to be financed. A member of the cabinet rose at that time and said: "On the basis of the information we have, the federal government will be making generous contributions". That was the expectation.
368	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Herridge
I want to refer to one or two conclusions in the British Columbia post-war rehabilitation council report. It has this to say with regard to market extension:
Market extension is promised on the conviction that one of the basic principles of reconstruction is that of increased world purchasing power.
Then it continues:
The post-war problems in British Columbia, as elsewhere, will be so complex and complicated they cannot be solved by the government alone. They require the fullest co-ordination between the three governments, federal, provincial and municipal.
I say without any hesitation, Mr. Speaker, that the people of British Columbia, working through their government and organizations representing various groups of people, farming and industrial, made these recommendations in the belief that this government was going to take the lead in a program of national and public investment in this country.
Their report continues-this is a very interesting sentence, in view of what has happened:
One of the other weaknesses of public policy in the last depression was that of public expenditures being too little and too late.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, that history will not repeat itself in that respect, although to a limited extent that is true today because if this government had its plans fully developed it could have relieved to a considerable extent the unemployment that exists in this country at this time, which does not result entirely from seasonal conditions.
What has been the attitude of this government with respect to full employment in the international sphere? I should like to draw to the attention of the house the recommendations of the United Nations which dealt with national and international measures for full employment. The United Nations assembly was urged through the economic and social council to take up the question of full employment and to put forth definite proposals for international projects designed to maintain full employment.
In December, 1949, the five economists to whom the secretary-general of the United Nations referred the matter presented their unanimous report. This report opens up tremendous possibilities and is entirely different from any report that would have been proposed under such auspices a few years ago. In view of the developing economic situation, what these leading economists asked for is an automatic system for the maintenance of world purchasing power to be brought into force at once upon the appearance of any serious signs of recession in any leading country. What they asked was that each 

country shall not only take on measures in its power to prevent a fall in its own domestic level of demand but that it shall guarantee to put at its disposal for the rest of the world a staple surplus of its own currency.
They contemplate the use of such funds largely for advancing development in the borrowing countries and they ask for drastic revision of the statutes of the international bank and of the international monetary fund.
The interesting point of these proposals is the recognition that private investment by the leading countries in the less developed countries is incapable of reaching the volume or stability that the maintenance of full employment requires, and that lending by governments to governments through a neutral international agency provides the only possible answer. That is very clear and definite in the report, and I have read it most carefully, Mr. Speaker.
What was the Canadian government's reaction to the proposals on an international level? As evidence that this government does not believe in international planning, or in domestic plans, to meet the problem of unemployment or markets I want to quote from the Montreal Gazette of January 20, 1950, which deals with the Canadian reaction to the proposals. It is headed:
Canada Snubs Jobless Plan UN Committee told Rigid Work Controls Impracticable Here
Lake Success, New York, January 19-Canada today told a United Nations economic group that rigid automatic measures to counter unemployment are not practicable for the Canadian economy.
John Deutsch, director of international economic relations in Canada's finance department, said Canada's economy is dependent largely on development of natural resources and sale of its products abroad. He said automatic readjustment of taxation and expenditures when unemployment threatens would therefore not be realistic for Canada.
He spoke before the fifteen-member economic and employment commission which is studying recent recommendations by a group of five top economic experts for global and national measures to maintain full employment.
Deutsch urged that the committee refrain from taking direct action on the recommendations, but circulate them among United Nations members requesting views of all governments on the problem.
Turning to the experts' proposals for international action, Deutsch said the unstable equilibrium of world trade and payments is of overriding importance for Canada.
Re-establishment of an adequate flow of international investments as proposed by the experts would be an excellent development, he said. But it does not appear likely in view of the present outlook, he added.
That is the end of the quotation from the Montreal Gazette. But it means this, that the Canadian representative turned down the proposals made by this committee of the

United Nations to deal with the question of full employment as a result of international planning.
What are we doing about the development of our markets? I see my time has almost expired, but before taking my seat I should like to say that anyone who is interested in the question of the marketing of agricultural products would be well advised to read the speech of the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch), as it is reported at page 190 of Hansard for February 23. As usual, the hon. member gave a most intelligent and comprehensive review of the situation.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) admits that the standard of living of eastern peoples must be raised and must be improved if democracy is to be developed in those areas. On the one hand we refuse opportunities to develop full employment through international planning and, on the other hand, we see people starving. Yet we admit that if democracy is to be developed these peoples must have access to our surplus products.
What has happened in that respect? We have world food plans. In September of 1946 Lord John Boyd Orr submitted his proposals for a world food board to stabilize agricultural prices of commodities on the world market, and included in those proposals the provision of funds for stabilizing functions, and so on. Time will not permit me to place on record all the details of his plan, but I would comment briefly by saying that the plan was rejected. Canada was elected to the world food council in September of 1947, but hope for the plan was smothered by a revision of these proposals. Nowhere do I find any evidence of Canada's having supported them.
Again, the conference of the International Federation of Agricultural Producers was held at Guelph in June, 1949, and made proposals for intergovernmental commodity agreements providing for an international agency which would deal with the commodities concerned.
In addition, the International Federation of Agricultural Producers recommended special action programs to move surpluses of agricultural products which already exist in certain countries to other countries where people remain ill fed and ill clothed because they lack the means of production and purchasing power. I find no evidence of Canada's having supported those proposals.
The meeting of the food and agricultural organization at Washington in November, 1949, made plans to establish an international commodity clearing house to channel agricultural surpluses into countries where food was
The Address-Mr. Herridge badly needed. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) has made it quite clear that this government is opposed to all such schemes. Referring to the international commodity clearing house the minister is reported to have said, "We don't need that; we can do it ourselves."
Without question our government has turned its back on proposals for international planning, for the creating of full employment and the marketing of world surpluses in what would be considered an unorthodox way.
What is the attitude of the farmer? I have not time to deal at length with that subject, but we do know that the farmers in this country are behind these proposals. The British Columbia fruit growers association at its last annual convention, in January, passed a resolution in which it heartily supported the action of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, and the resolution passed by that federation was in these words:
Whereas the FAO international commodity clearing house seeks to establish:
1.	The maintenance of a high level of production and employment.
2.	The reduction of trade restrictions, including tariffs and quantitative and monetary restrictions.
3.	An increase in the standards of productive efficiency, particularly in western Europe.
4.	International investment to finance export and import surpluses and
5.	The restoration of convertible currencies and multilateral transactions as a basis of world trade- all of which is designed to feed properly an undernourished world and thus utilize all presently available and potential food and fibre production.
Therefore, the British Columbia Fruit Growers' Association in its 1950 annual convention commends the Canadian Federation of Agriculture for promoting so effectively the world food pool principle and the sixty-one countries which make up FAO for planning to put this world-essential principle into active operation, and urges the Canadian government to give this project its complete support.
The fruit growers of British Columbia are keenly interested in this proposal, because they are facing a serious situation in connection with the returns from this year's crop and the disposal of the new crop. I shall not deal at length with this phase of the matter because the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Jones) intends to do so later in the debate.
To maintain our markets I support the proposal of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) that, instead of demanding payment in dollars by the sterling area, we accept more goods and part payment in sterling, and the reinvestment of this sterling in the undeveloped sterling areas. That is not a complete solution, but it is an immediate approach to the present world economic difficulties.
In addition to that, we support international planning along the lines suggested by the

The Address-Mr. Herridge international commodity clearing house tor the distribution of our greatly required agricultural surpluses.
In addition to that, and above all, I am sure if we are going to play our part in the restoration of the world economy we will find that in some cases it will be necessary to make gifts to certain countries. I should like to see agricultural surpluses disposed of in that way, and paid for out of taxation, rather than see large sums being spent on unemployment relief. By being able to produce we will maintain morale and do something effective towards solving economic questions.
Before taking my seat I should like to speak briefly about unemployment. At this time we have in Canada about 400,000 unemployed -these are the numbers registered. We have these unemployed, despite our great natural resources, and our great human resources. How does this figure compare with those of the United States and Great Britain? The latest figures for Great Britain show 329,000 unemployed, a labour force of 23 million, and a percentage of 1-4 unemployed. Similar figures for the United States show 4,800,000 jobless, with a labour force of 60 million, and a percentage of unemployed of 7-5. On the basis of 323,000 jobless and a labour force of 5-1 million, Canada has a percentage of 6-3 unemployed.
What about Australia and New Zealand? They are both in a position quite different from ours. There is full employment in New Zealand; and on the basis of information radioed from Australia today they have about
1.000	registered unemployed; but they have
107.000	jobs for which applicants cannot De found.
Let us compare the position in Australia with that of Canada. Here we have greater natural resources and greater opportunities. I will admit that we have seasonal unemployment, a form of unemployment which can be taken care of through the use of the Unemployment Insurance Act. Over and above that however, as evidenced by the mounting numbers of unemployed in the early fall months, we have in this country a genuine unemployment situation which has no relationship to weather conditions.
We believe that the government should1 give effect to the promises it has made commencing in 1945, and should develop public investment policies which can only be successfully developed as the result of planning over a period of time. That is my major criticism of the government. These projects were not planned and developed so that they could be put into operation when the need arose. We know now that the government is proceeding

with the proposal for a trans-Canada highway. It is making expenditures under the Canada Forestry Act, as well as other departmental expenditures. Nevertheless the bare fact is that at this time there are thousands of Canadians unemployed and wasting their ability to labour because the government has not put into effect plans to put them to work.
I now want to deal with my own constituency for a few minutes. In Kootenay West at the present time there are about 2,000 registered unemployed. I admit that undoubtedly some of these men are seasonally unemployed, but I think if the government had given previous consideration to the question many of them could have been working to the advantage of Canada. I suggest that there are projects which are feasible in the winter months. I will admit there are difficulties in the wintertime in carrying out certain types of projects in some parts of Canada, but for the information of the house I shall give a few projects that with proper planning could be undertaken in the district I represent in order to absorb those who are unemployed at this time. For instance, we need a million dollar expenditure on the extension of the river wall alongside the Columbia river to protect the city of Trail. I am not going to lay the primary blame on the dominion government in that respect because I believe the principle the government has established is sound, namely, that provincial governments should place their plans before the dominion government. I believe that the municipalities should deal with the problems first, and that the province concerned should make application on behalf of the municipality. The government has a sound reason for saying that nothing has been done because the provincial government of British Columbia has failed to make suggestions to the federal government as to the need for the building of a river wall at Trail.
Then there is other work in unincorporated areas along the Columbia river which could well be done in the wintertime. In previous years it has been done then. I refer to the prevention of erosion of the banks of the Columbia river at certain points. We also need a new federal building at Trail, but to construct such a building in order to absorb the unemployed in a certain period of the year requires previous planning and, shall I say, an abnormal direction of effort. We also need a new federal building at Nelson. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that these are some of the things that could be accomplished in my own constituency even during the winter months.
I have not time to speak about clause 2 of the amendment to the amendment which criticizes the government for not introducing an over-all security program. One is fully

justified in supporting clauses 1 and 2 of the amendment to the amendment because the present government has not brought before the house proposals for an over-all security program. Are we going to continue to waste our human and natural resources? In the direction of our economic affairs are we going to continue to accept what I would term the philosophy of the money-changers who still have control of the economic policies of the western world? On the other hand, are we going to justify our claim to be a Christian democracy by using our human and natural resources to the advantage of Canadians and of alb mankind? In view of the record of the government and the evidence and facts before us, I think the house would be fully justified in supporting the amendment to the amendment.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the first time I have risen to speak in the house. As one of the junior members on the government side, with only five weeks in the house during the last session and two weeks during this session, I want to say it is a real privilege for me to have the opportunity of expressing my thoughts and views to the house, and also certain ideas I have which may be of some benefit to the whole of the great Dominion of Canada. First of all, I should like to join in the congratulations and expressions of appreciation that have been extended to the mover (Mr. Larson) and seconder (Mr. Dumas) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I am certain I could not find words to add to those which have already been uttered in commendation of them. I am sure we are all proud of these two young members and that we all look forward to hearing from them on many occasions in the future.
I have the honour to represent the constituency of New Westminster, which includes three large municipalities in the surrounding area. Over twenty years ago Senator Tom Reid, the previous member for that district, came here as a new member of the house. No doubt on first entering the house he put forward his views as to his constituency. Therefore I think it is only right and proper that I should say something on behalf of my constituents. Hon. members presume, when a member rises to speak about his constituency, he has some knowledge of his subject. Before dealing with that question, on behalf of the citizens of New Westminster and the surrounding district I should like to say how much they appreciate the honour that has been conferred upon Senator Tom Reid by his elevation to the Senate. He served his early term as an apprentice in this house faithfully and well. I am sure
The Address-Mr. Mott the people I represent would want me to convey to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) our appreciation of and thanks for this worthy appointment.
New Westminster is an industrial city and includes the port of New Westminster, the fastest growing fresh water port in the Dominion of Canada today. It is an export and import point, and very little coastal shipping goes in and out of there. Within the bounds of the city there are many industries. We have some of the largest lumber mills in the British empire. There is salmon fishing on the Fraser river, and we have the great salmon canning industry employing about 20,000 of our people. Across the river we have three rural municipalities, Surrey, Delta and Langley, whose main pursuit is farming. They run approximately fifty miles inland along the south bank of the Fraser river, and are bounded on one side by the river and on the other by the international boundary. I mention these three municipalities together with my own city for the simple reason that there are very few things which come up in this house which do not affect them in one way or another. In that district I believe we also have the largest poultry farming area in British Columbia.
I come here, Mr. Speaker, not with experience with the senior government but having municipal experience and the municipal point of view. I served on the council for five years, and as mayor of New Westminster for six years, and for a term as president of the union of British Columbia municipalities. After having spent so much time in municipal life naturally my feelings today are for municipal governments. Therefore I should like to devote part of my time to some of the problems facing the municipalities today.
I listened with a great deal of interest to the previous speaker, who dealt with many of the things I had intended to mention. However, I shall try to elaborate on them from my personal experience. One of the first things I should like to deal with is the financial set-up in the municipalities. No doubt you are all well acquainted with the means by which the municipalities do their financing. Land taxation seems to be the main: source of revenue, though certain large cities have a business tax, while others have public utilities from which they derive certain benefits. In the main, however, their revenue comes from the land; and when under provincial legislation education is left to the municipalities, it means that education must be paid for by taxes imposed on land.
During the recess I visited several municipalities in the west, and for a moment I should like to touch upon one point in regard

The Address-Mr. Mott to unemployment. Much work could be provided by the municipalities if they had ways and means of raising the money to pay for it. As the previous speaker mentioned, it is only too true that a municipality must approach this government through the provincial government, because the province is asked to be responsible for the finances of its municipalities. That prompts me to suggest that we should bring back the municipal aid act that was discontinued in 1937. There is no doubt that if this aid were given today it would go far toward helping the municipalities take care of their unemployed, and thus assist in alleviating the unemployment situation that exists today. This aid was given at a time when unemployment was at a low level. Such work as ditching, brushing and similar projects could be found in any municipality. I realize that this assistance must be applied for through the provincial government; I understand that the municipalities of British Columbia are requesting the government of that province to apply for that aid once more. I am making the same request now, so that if possible the municipalities may have that assistance now or in the immediate future.
I think we all agree that the strongest link in our chain of government is the municipal government. At the last dominion-provincial conference some of the municipalities were left out. I believe some of the provincial governments took their municipalities into their confidence before going to the conference, but that was not the case with all provinces. We in British Columbia were not allowed to submit any requests to our government to be brought forward at that time. I do not see how we can change the constitution of this country as it affects the general dominion-provincial set-up without in some way interfering with the provincial-municipal set-up as well. So I suggest that when the next dominion-provincial conference is held this government should see to it that a representative group from the mayors' association is given an opportunity to present their views, in the form of a brief or otherwise, before final agreements are reached.
As one instance of what I have in mind in this connection I might mention the amusement tax which this government took over during the war. When that tax was dropped most of the provincial governments imposed it for their own benefit. Personally I believe that when the dominion government dropped that tax it intended that it should go back to the municipalities. In a municipality, say the council is called upon to submit a bylaw to the people to find the money to put up a

skating rink or other recreational centre, which may be of value in improving the health of our future citizens, but the ratepayers are still burdened with a 25 per cent amusement tax that was then imposed, merely because professional hockey or baseball is being played there. I am citing one instance to more or less substantiate what I was saying about dominion-provincial-municipal relations.
I should like to say a word about the housing act that was passed last year. In all sincerity, I congratulate the government upon the institution of an act which will do something towards supplying these badly needed homes. I believe that these houses can be of greater benefit in the large urban centres than they can in our fast-growing rural areas. During the recess I had an opportunity of speaking to the representatives of various municipalities. I learned that the big problem in opening up land for building purposes is not the question of repayment of the cost of the necessary utilities, but the question of schools. The building of new homes in communities that are already overcrowded only means increasing an already heavy school burden. I think perhaps this government should do something towards helping to finance these schools.
As one who has served on a municipal council, I should like to take this opportunity of thanking the government for recognizing crown lands and granting assistance in lieu of taxation. It may not be just what we wanted, but at the same time it is a step in the right direction. Action in this direction has been long overdue, and I feel that in starting with the thin edge of the wedge, the government may be induced to go further in helping the municipalities pay for the services that have been such a burden to municipal ratepayers.
I have listened, Mr. Speaker, with a great deal of interest to the many speakers in this house. Since I am a new member and do not know many of them, it is rather difficult to grasp their ideas, or the criticisms which they have aimed at the government. Listening to the speeches here reminded me of the years I spent as a trade unionist, listening to many interesting speeches about the law of supply and demand. Any man who could solve that problem would be held in the highest esteem. As one listens to this debate, one is reminded of the many occasions upon which we have seemed to be on the point of solving that problem, but apparently because something has been left out of the formula, we dropped back. It seems to me that if we could only solve that problem we would be able to go forward at much greater speed,.

It is my intention today to try to offer some few suggestions, first of all, about unemployment. I believe we must look forward to a properly planned program. If we had such a program from one end of Canada to the other, it would go a long way towards solving the unemployment problem. We understand that most of the unemployment today is of a seasonal nature. Nevertheless, we do not know exactly when something more serious is going to happen, and if we have not a program we may be called upon to pay out millions of dollars in the dole. In connection with this planned program,
I believe we could follow the lead of the many municipalities that have adopted town planning programs. That is on a small scale, but we could probably follow some such plan from one end of the dominion to the other.
I should like to mention some of the things which should fit into such a planned program, as I see it from looking at conditions in my own constituency. First of all, it will be necessary to have a certain amount of building construction throughout Canada, regardless of the area or whether it is done by private enterprise, the dominion government or the provincial government. The dominion and provincial programs should be lined up to fit in with the number of trades we have in Canada. If we knew the number of trades that would be involved in any depression, some kind of program could be worked out. I do not believe in this idea of putting advertisements in the paper every spring for tenders on public buildings. I believe that work should be spread over a period of time, and the places selected in which it is necessary to give employment.
I should like to say a few words about another problem that I believe faces us on the Pacific coast. It is something that should be planned for, and that is our export-import trade. What are we doing or what are we going to do for the necessary facilities to handle these cargoes? For instance, in the port of New Westminster we have nine docks. Before the war the largest number of deep-sea ships that ever came into that port was about 550. We are now faced with this problem of trade that we expect will arise with the Far East-that is, with Japan and China- from which most of the trade to that port came before the war. I am certain that the present dock facilities in the port of New Westminster will never be able to handle that trade, and I am quite certain that Vancouver today has not the facilities to handle it. I am only mentioning this matter because it is something else that no doubt should be planned, so that money could be loaned and we would know just where we were going.
The Address-Mr. Mott
I should like to mention another matter which I believe would be of some help to the growth of this country, and which I believe should be investigated; I refer to the matter of a free port or free zone or free warehousing in the various ports of Canada today. We have heard many speakers on this particular problem. We know that in Seattle there is a certain area for this purpose, but I do not believe that Canada has ever gone into the question and made a thorough investigation of a free port or free zone or free warehousing in order to build up our ports. It is not a new thing. It is over two hundred1 years old on the European continent, but I do not believe that we have ever gone into it, to find out whether it would be of benefit to us or not.
Another matter that I believe we should investigate thoroughly is that of railways, not only those nationally-owned but also the ones owned by the provinces. I am not speaking with regard to any other, province than British Columbia. At the present time we have a railway starting from a certain point and1 going a certain distance. There is no doubt that it is the intention of the provincial government to finish the railway which will be of great benefit not only to British Columbia but also to the Dominion of Canada. As to planning the final stages of that railway, I believe it should be done in- conjunction with the federal government here, with our Department of National Defence and perhaps with our friends across the border in the United States. It may not be necessary to call in all those bodies but it is my belief that in planning for the future that is something that certainly should be taken into consideration.
As to unemployment, I have just this one other suggestion to offer with regard to a planned program of work to be done, and *that is a tunnel across the mouth of the Fraser river. Here is a project valued at around $6 million or $7 million. It may not have any direct bearing on the dominion government, but it has on the provincial government. In planning for the future, here is one project that should be given consideration at the present time. An organization of some 350 members and several of our municipalities request this tunnel. The only thing they ask for is $10,000 for a proper survey. The tunnel, which would be paid for by tolls, would give employment to thousands at the present time. It is a project that would cost in the neighbourhood of $5 million or $6 million. It is almost impossible to find out where the help would come from with regard to getting such a project started.
I am not going to say any more at this time, Mr. Speaker. I have a great deal of material before me, such as press clippings. It was my thought at the start that I would endeavour
j74	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Shaw to speak for forty minutes, this being the first time that I have offered a word at all in this house. As time goes on, however, and as I become more acquainted with the proceedings, I am certain that you will hear further from me. I think I can say on behalf of my own constituency that we appreciate what the government have done and the good work they are doing at the present time. I am sure that the program' enunciated during the last election will be fulfilled. The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), in his very able speech on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, mentioned that the promises made during the election would no doubt be fulfilled; at the present time some of them have been fulfilled. I am not going to say anything more, except that I am glad to have this opportunity to address the house, and I hope that some of the suggestions I have made will be given serious attention by the government.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
At the commencement of my remarks this afternoon, Mr. Speaker, I should1 like to extend congratulations to the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I believe that all of us who heard the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Larson) and the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Dumas) will agree that they acquitted themselves in a commendable fashion.
The throne speech itself covers a wide range of subjects. I noted, among other things, reference to the conference with the representatives of the provinces, housing, the trans-Canada highway, international affairs, national defence, employment and unemployment, trade, rent control, veterans legislation, revision of the Indian Act, and so forth. A number of those subjects have already been debated rather extensively during this session, ft is not my desire nor my intention to endeavour to cover them all. In fact, in the forepart of my remarks I intend to depart from them almost entirely. The reference to the Indian Act may have taken my mind back to something which I brought before the House of Commons on December 9 last. Hon. members who were here on that occasion may recall that we were considering the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare, Indian health services, and I brought before the house then a specific problem of great importance. It is true that the problem related specifically to my own constituency and affected approximately 350 persons, namely, the treaty Indians of the Sunchild Cree reservation and the non-treaty Chippewa Indians of that area. In the course of my observations in December I laid emphasis upon the extremely appalling health conditions which then prevailed among that 

group of people, and they still prevail. I attributed these conditions to a number of things, among which were inadequate housing and no plans for properly executed enterprise, but above all else, Mr. Speaker, no plans to conduct a comprehensive health survey among these people. Upon that occasion I had intended to deal in great detail with exactly what had taken place during recent months and recent years, and to present to this house a comprehensive analysis of the problem from every conceivable angle. But the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) rendered such a task on my part unnecessary-at least I thought it was unnecessary-when he interjected the following words which are recorded in Hansard for December 9, at page 3008. I would remind hon. members that he interjected after I had spoken for ten or fifteen minutes:
I wonder if I might say a word, after which my hon. friend may not find it necessary to go a great deal further. He will recall bringing this matter to my attention earlier. As a result a survey was undertaken, and a nurse is to be appointed. We had hoped to get her out there quickly, but she has to leave another post to follow up on that survey. I want to thank my hon. friend for bringing the matter to my attention. I can say also that arrangements have been made with the doctors there which I believe are satisfactory. Following my hon. friend's suggestions I think he will find that we are taking corrective action.
I expressed my appreciation to the minister and to the government and I said that I would not go further upon that occasion. After all, what I was seeking was a solution, but I did conclude by saying this:
I shall go among these Indians and talk to the doctors and the nurse.
The minister said:
I hope you will keep me advised. If not, I shall go out there myself.
Last month I did spend a good deal of time out there and what I learned could cause me to be caustically critical today, but rather my speech will be delivered in an atmosphere of sorrow, sorrow for being taken in the way I was last December.
On January 9 and January 10 and again on January 28 and 29 I went into the Rocky Mountain House district. I conferred with the doctors, I conferred with hospital authorities, I conferred with many persons in town,
I conferred with a number of the Cree and the Chippewa Indians, and I learned this: First, that no arrangements whatsoever had been made with the doctors. To this day they have not had the scratch of a pen from the Department of National Health and Welfare relative to that matter. Second, no arrangement has been made with the municipal hospital for the admission of Indian patients; in fact, they are being excluded in the absence of an agreement. Third, there

was no evidence of any health survey being undertaken, unless it can be said that for a nurse to come into town one day, which is thirty miles from the reservation, and go out the next, is a health survey. Personally, such could not be considered by me as being an acceptable survey at all.
Obviously the Minister of National Health and Welfare has some explaining to do. I realize that he cannot have a personal knowledge of everything that goes on within every branch of his department. I will concede that point. He must depend upon the information which is conveyed to him by the authorities of the various branches within his department. Possibly he was taken in. In any event there is some explaining to do, or else he is going to experience some difficulty in getting out of doing what he said he might have to do, namely, go in there himself.
May I emphasize, Mr. Speaker, what I said upon that occasion, namely, the desperately bad situation among these people. It is not only these people who are affected. Some of them are in town every day, and they are circulating among the white people. Let me remind the house that it is estimated 50 per cent have tuberculosis, and it is conceded that an equally large number are inflicted with venereal disease.
It is conceivable that the Minister of National Health and Welfare, or the officials of his department, may have negotiated arrangements with doctors other than those in the town of Rocky Mountain House. That was not the implication in the statement that was made last fall, because I mentioned the doctors by name. It is conceivable that they may have made some type of arrangement for hospitalization elsewhere than in the vicinity; it is also conceivable that they may have a health survey in operation; but it is one of these things that certainly it is impossible for anyone to detect.
Let me emphasize, the logical place for these people to be treated is locally. The logical place for them to be hospitalized, except of course in advanced cases of tuberculosis and so on, would be there. I would say in cases of tuberculosis the patients should be taken to the Charles Camsell hospital. That would be the proper place for them to be treated. The effect of the failure to negotiate an agreement with the hospital and doctors in this area simply means that 98 per cent of the patients are beyond hope when they reach the Charles Camsell hospital in Edmonton.
Last fall I read case histories of people ranging in age from five years to thirty-six. Those reports would almost make one's blood run cold. I am not going to take further time upon that matter. I trust that the Minister
The Address-Mr. Shaw of National Health and Welfare will be prepared to take action in this matter. If not I am going to press the matter upon every conceivable occasion that I can squeeze it in. I trust that at least before this session of parliament is over we shall be able to say that some concrete action has been taken to solve this problem.
On the same day, December 9, we were discussing the Indian affairs branch, which came under the Department of Mines and Resources at that time. I referred to this health situation and said to the Minister of Mines and Resources: "It will be extremely necessary for the officials of the Indian Affairs branch to give serious and thoughtful consideration to the responsibilities that rest upon them in this connection." At that time I referred to the question of the Chippewa Indians refusing, up to that date, to accept treaty. From what later took place, Mr. Speaker, I know that my remarks were misunderstood, at least in one quarter. I criticized the actions of someone, whom I did not desire to name, in the method of dealing with these Chippewa Indians. At that time I was referring to the former Indian agent, and I was not referring to anyone else. I stated at that time that I was not satisfied with the operation of the agency at that point, and I was not satisfied with the economic aspect of the problem as related to those Indians. I want to pay tribute to the former Minister of Mines and Resources, because he at least took the first and most essential step.
The new agent at Rocky Mountain House possesses, I believe, the experience and knowledge necessary to qualify him for his position. We feel, too, that his generally sympathetic attitude towards the problem will commend him for that post. We hope he will be able to meet and to solve the many acute problems which have existed for too long. But his success or failure will depend upon two things: To an appreciable extent it will depend, first, upon government policy and, secondly, upon the degree of co-operation he receives from his superiors.
I went right into the reservation, which is thirty miles from the town of Rocky Mountain House. It is a heavily timbered area. Upon that occasion I had what is sometimes called a powwow with the Indians themselves, and here are a few of the things I learned from personal observation and from discussion with them. I should hope my comments would be conveyed to the officials of the Indian affairs branch.
I learned, first, that the Indians in that area are asking for only one thing, and that is the opportunity to be self-supporting. May I add in passing that there is very

The Address-Mr. Shaw little evidence of any encouragement being given to them, a feature which is most essential if they are to become self-supporting. There must be an appropriation for livestock. Some time I am going to inquire as to the exact amount of money spent in there. Lands must be cleared under supervision in order to provide feed for the livestock-and I use the word "cleared" because this is a wooded area. Nothing could be more appalling to the individual than to see what I saw there-livestock dying from lack of feed. Nothing could be more discouraging for the Indians than to clear land, as many of them did, on which feed could be grown, and then to have that ground stand for three or four years, and not have it inspected or approved for breaking until the end of the four years. Then it is broken in October. I am sure the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) will appreciate what happens to land when it is broken at a time when frost is setting in at night, in the month of October.
There must be supervision in the matter of home construction. It is ridiculous to make appropriations for home construction in that area, and then permit to happen that which has happened. Many of these homes have been spoiled because no one has told the Indians how to mix cement. It is mighty hard to stomach a situation where windows, doors, roofing materials and other building materials have been left out in the open for two years, and have deteriorated to a point where they are valueless. These are materials which, I presume, were purchased for the use of the Indians.
Here is one of the worst features of the whole thing. It is estimated that there are 25 million feet of merchantable timber on that reservation-and I have that figure from an expert lumberman. If that timber were farmed, as we say, those Indians would have a million feet of lumber per year for the next twenty-five years, or a half million for the next fifty years. But that timber is
now being murdered-and I can think of no other suitable term. They have a saw mill just outside the reservation, operated by a white man-and incidentally he is one of the best, and is one hundred per cent interested in the Indians. However, he has no authority to set foot on the reservation.
Those Indians are in there cutting the timber, and it would look as though they are just shutting their eyes and swinging their axes. The result is that they are leaving some of the best timber, the large trees, to blow over, after they have taken the rest of it. They have been given no guidance in this matter, with the result that the cost of moving the logs out and making the lumber is almost prohibitive.
Surely it is not too much to ask the department to give the Indians the instruction and advice which is necessary if they are to make the best possible use of that timber. I suggested last fall, and I repeat it today, that assistance should be given to enable them to take one or more smaller, portable saw mills in on the reservation.
I understand some steps are being taken in the matter of education, but little progress is being made. The Indians have been instructed to cut logs about thirty feet long for a school but I doubt very much if they will ever be able to get them out to the proper place, because there is no supervision in their cutting.
As it is almost six o'clock, and I could not possibly finish before that time, I would move the adjournment of the debate.
Motion (Mr. Shaw) agreed to and debate adjourned.
